title: You've Never Seen Your Own Eyes Move #brain #science
description:
Look in a mirror and switch from your left eye to your right: you never see them move. They do: in quick jumps called saccades, several times a second. Around each jump your brain suppresses what you see, hiding the blur, and stitches the views together. A phone's front camera shows its picture a split second late, so the movement reaches the screen after the jump is over, and you see it.

More on how cameras and brains see motion: Why do wheels spin backwards on camera? https://youtu.be/SxjS9sdc_Ek

Sources
- Erdmann, B. & Dodge, R. (1898), Psychologische Untersuchungen über das Lesen (first report that we never see our own eye movements)
- Bach, M., Saccadic Suppression, Visual Phenomena & Optical Illusions (michaelbach.de): the mirror and selfie-camera demonstration
- Idrees, S. et al. (2020), Perceptual saccadic suppression starts in the retina, Nature Communications 11: 1977
- Binda, P. & Morrone, M. C. (2018), Vision during saccadic eye movements, Annual Review of Vision Science 4: 193–213

Try it: mirror first, then your phone's front camera. Did you catch them?
